questions: You have been asked to transmit a crucial skill to a visitor who leaves at dawn, but the body-to-body teaching traditionally happens only when the dew is on the grass. The visitor insists their departure cannot change. What costs you more internally: breaking the seasonal timing or letting the transmission remain incomplete?

You encounter a practice you have never seen before—neither clearly from your lineage nor obviously foreign. It sits in the threshold space between seasons. Do you find yourself first reaching for the silence required to let it reveal its origins, or do you feel compelled to name it immediately to protect the clarity of what belongs here?

Two kin members are in open dispute over land use, speaking in the heated language of rights and ownership. The tension is spilling into the collective gathering. What feels more necessary to your body: withdrawing to let the conflict season underground until a story emerges that can reframe their positions into kinship terms, or stepping in now to stop the bleeding before it poisons the gathering?

You are required to document a living practice using standardized forms that strip away the tactile, seasonal, and kinship contexts, reducing it to checkboxes and timestamps. Imagine you must choose one connection to sever for a full year: either access to the oldest living elder who holds the deepest silences, or access to the youth who receive skills through your body-to-body transmission. Which absence settles heavier in your bones?

If all obligations were lifted for one full cycle—no transmissions due, no disputes to season, no outsiders seeking interpretation—where would your body drift? Toward the solitude of the terrain where you might listen without speaking, or toward the gathering where you might weave the stories that hold the collective center?

You have limited energy to preserve a fragile skill. You can either create a detailed record that will outlast your body but cannot breathe or adapt, or you can spend that same energy transmitting it living and responsive to one kin member who may adapt it beyond recognition. Which use of your limited breath feels more faithful?

You have committed to guiding a kin member through a seasonal threshold ritual that requires your full bodily presence for three days, but an institutional authority demands your signature on documents that would legitimize your role within their system—documents that expire before the ritual concludes. What hollows you out more: disappointing the kinship network that trusts your body, or remaining illegible to the structures that could protect your terrain?

A stranger presents you with data showing that a practice you have always done in one specific watershed is causing ecological harm according to their measurements. Your body knows the practice as reciprocal with the land, but their numbers are compelling. Do you first seek the silence to let your body confirm what the terrain knows, or do you feel compelled to engage their abstract system on its own terms to prove your care?

An outsider has violated a protocol in your terrain, causing harm that cannot be undone. The institutional system offers a formal process of restitution that would close the matter efficiently, while your kinship network demands a slower, embodied reconciliation that might never achieve closure. Which path feels more dangerous to your sense of belonging: the efficiency that resolves without healing, or the endless openness of kinship reckoning?

You are forbidden from speaking the old language during official gatherings, where only the standardized tongue is permitted. You must convey something that only the old words can hold. A practice you transmit is becoming irrelevant to the daily lives of youth, who face new pressures from the outside world. You can adapt the practice to address their present struggles, knowing this will change its essential character, or you can preserve it exactly as received, knowing they may abandon it as useless. Which betrayal of your obligation keeps you awake at night: the adaptation that alters, or the preservation that loses?
